Are LLMs Ready to Replace Bangla Annotators?

Md. Najib Hasan Affiliation:  A2I Lab, School of Computing, Wichita State University Email: mxhasan39@shockers.wichita.edu    Touseef Hasan Affiliation:  A2I Lab, School of Computing, Wichita State University Email: txhasan4@shockers.wichita.edu    Souvika Sarkar Affiliation:  A2I Lab, School of Computing, Wichita State University Email: souvika.sarkar@wichita.edu
Abstract

Large Language Models (LLMs) are increasingly used as automated annotators to scale dataset creation, yet their reliability as unbiased annotators—especially for low-resource and identity-sensitive settings—remains poorly understood. In this work, we study the behavior of LLMs as zero-shot annotators for Bangla hate speech, a task where even human agreement is challenging, and annotator bias can have serious downstream consequences. We conduct a systematic benchmark of 17 LLMs using a unified evaluation framework. Our analysis uncovers annotator bias and substantial instability in model judgments. Surprisingly, increased model scale does not guarantee improved annotation quality—smaller, more task-aligned models frequently exhibit more consistent behavior than their larger counterparts. These results highlight important limitations of current LLMs for sensitive annotation tasks in low-resource languages and underscore the need for careful evaluation before deployment.

1 Introduction

High-quality data annotation is a critical yet increasingly unsustainable bottleneck in modern natural language processing (NLP) research. As online text continues to grow, the demand for labeled data has far outpaced what human annotators can reasonably produce. Manual annotation is slow, expensive Snow et al. (2008), and often inconsistent, with even trained annotators frequently disagreeing Hartvigsen et al. (2022). To address these limitations, recent work has explored the use of LLMs for large-scale data annotation Gilardi et al. (2023). Despite their efficiency, LLM-based annotation raises a central concern: annotator bias Lucy and Bamman (2021). As LLMs are trained on massive web corpora that encode societal stereotypes, cultural imbalances, and skewed viewpoints, they may systematically propagate these biases into their labeling decisions Das et al. (2024); Bender et al. (2021).

Prior studies have largely examined these issues in high-resource languages such as English Liang et al. (2022); Gehman et al. (2020). In contrast, annotator bias in LLM-based annotation for low-resource languages (e.g., Bangla) remains largely unexplored. This gap is further exacerbated by—limited annotation guidelines, scarcity of expert annotators, and uneven dataset quality. In this work, we investigate annotator bias in LLMs when applied to zero-shot annotation of Bangla hate speech. Hate speech presents a particularly challenging and informative testbed due to its inherently subjective nature, as judgments are shaped by cultural norms, social context, and identity-specific sensitivities Sap et al. (2019). Even subtle biases in this domain can significantly affect annotation outcomes and downstream decisions. Rather than treating LLMs as black-box classifiers, we analyze their reliability as unbiased annotators by examining consistency on identity-sensitive inputs and robustness across different prompting conditions. Specifically, we address the following research questions:

RQ 1. Can LLMs reliably identify identity-sensitive hate speech in a low-resource language like Bangla?

RQ 2. Can LLMs generate consistent and trustworthy reasoning in settings where even human annotators struggle to agree?

To answer these questions, we make the following contributions:

  • •

    We introduced a new Bangla hate speech dataset comprising 5,000 human-curated samples, spanning 21 identity-sensitive categories (e.g., Female, Hindu, Artist, etc.) which represent the individuals’ identities directly referenced in the text. These categories are grouped under five domains (e.g., Gender, Religion, Politics, etc.), enabling a structured analysis of both identity-specific bias and cross-domain generalization in LLM-based annotation.

  • •

    Proposed a novel unified evaluation framework that assesses model behavior across three dimensions: (i) classification performance, (ii) reasoning consistency, and (iii) robustness to prompt variation.

  • •

    Using our evaluation framework benchmarked 17 state-of-the-art LLMs for Bangla hate speech annotation, evaluating their reliability as automated annotators in a low-resource language.

Our results reveal a widespread bias of the annotator, frequent confusion of labels and strong sensitivity to minor variations in prompt (instruction) wording, highlighting the fundamental limitations of current LLMs as annotators. Results also show that larger models do not consistently produce more reliable annotations; in several cases, smaller and more task-aligned models exhibit greater stability and coherence.

2 Related Work

2.1 LLMs as Automated Annotators

LLMs are increasingly used as annotators in NLP due to their strong generalization ability and capacity to generate context-aware outputs He et al. (2023). Many studies aim to replace human annotators with LLMs to reduce reliance on scarce domain experts and lower the cost and time of manual annotation Zhang et al. (2023). Prior work reports promising results when LLMs are combined with techniques such as active learning and carefully designed instructions Huang et al. (2023). Prompting strategies have been explored to enable LLMs to act as labelers for sentiment analysis, toxicity detection, topic classification Gilardi et al. (2023), and zero-shot multi-label topic inference Sarkar et al. (2023); Sarkar et al. (2025). Some studies suggest that, with proper prompt tuning, LLMs can match or even outperform crowd workers in tasks such as stance detection and emotion labeling Wang et al. (2023). However, other research highlights the instability of LLM-based annotation, showing that minor prompt variations can lead to label shifts and inconsistent reasoning across similar examples Tornberg (2023). Additionally, LLMs often rely on surface-level cues and overlook deeper context, particularly in domains requiring specialized knowledge or morally sensitive judgment, which degrades performance on subjective tasks such as hate speech detection and sarcasm annotation Peng et al. (2024).

2.2 Inconsistency in LLM-based Annotation

Another major concern is hallucination, where LLMs fabricate labels or explanations without factual grounding Zhang et al. (2023). Bias also remains a persistent issue, as models trained primarily on public web data tend to reproduce social and cultural stereotypes, leading to distorted annotations Jadhav et al. (2024). Moreover, LLMs generally perform better in high-resource languages such as English, which benefit from abundant training data and large web corpora Mohta et al. (2023), while performance degrades substantially in low-resource languages including Bangla, Turkish, and Marathi Gu et al. (2025). This disparity stems from the underrepresentation of these languages in training data Nasution and Onan (2024).

2.3 Low-Resource Hate Speech Detection

In hate speech detection, LLMs are widely used to identify harmful online content Lucy and Bamman (2021). While they perform well on explicit hate, they often struggle with implicit or subtle forms Bender et al. (2021). Annotator bias is common, particularly in cases involving gender, religion, or political identity Liang et al. (2022). Even small prompt variations can lead to large output shifts without careful validation.

For Bangla, transformer-based models such as BanglaHateBERT Jahan et al. (2022), BanglaBERT Kowsher et al. (2022), and G-BERT Keya and others (2023) improve hate speech detection using language-specific data but are limited by scarce annotations. Recent work evaluates LLMs on Bangla hate speech with zero-shot and few-shot prompting Faria et al. (2024). However, performance remains unstable due to prompt sensitivity, hallucination, difficulty with Bangla-specific expressions Das et al. (2023), and bias in identities Das et al. (2024). These issues raise ethical concerns in hate speech detection Sadhu et al. (2024).

2.4 Uniqueness of Our Work

Unlike prior studies that focus on improving model accuracy or prompt design in isolation, our work integrates insights from all three research directions: LLMs as annotators, inconsistency in LLMs, and low-resource hate speech detection into a unified benchmarking framework. We systematically evaluate 17 LLMs on Bangla hate speech annotation, spanning 21 identity-based categories across five domains using classification accuracy, reasoning alignment, and prompt stability, on a novel dataset of 5,000 text samples in Bangla.

3 Problem Statement

Our goal is to find a well-aligned LLM-annotator that will give an unbiased decision with neutral reasons, regardless of the annotator’s identity. We design a framework which takes input: a text xx, annotator’s identity gg, a set of labels LL, and four levels of prompt ℓ∈{P​1,…,P​4}\ell\in\{P1,\dots,P4\}. Each data sample also contains an annotated human gold label yy and gold standard reasoning rr. We change only the annotator’s identity string denoted as gg, for example, “You are a Bangla hate-speech annotator with identity = Female” (repeated with Male). An LLM ff returns a predicted label y^\hat{y} and the reasons r^\hat{r} to support that predicted label as justification:

(y^,r^)=f⁡(x,g,ℓ,L)(\hat{y},\hat{r})\;=\;f(x,g,\ell,L)

The predicted label and the reasoning for that given sample should be the same in context if that specific LLM is unbiased and insensitive to identity.

For instance (as illustrated in Figure 1), the text “পাপন কে জুতা দিয়ে পিটিয়ে বিসিবি থেকে বের করে দেয়া হউক” (Let Papon be beaten with shoes and thrown out of the BCB) is given as input to an LLM with a set of labels: Offensive, Harassment, Violence, Propaganda, Not Hateful. By altering the annotator’s identity in the input prompt from Male to Female, if the LLM’s output label changes from Harassment to Not Hateful, it is an evidence of annotator bias in that specific LLM. On the contrary, if the output label doesn’t change even after changing the annotator identity, it means that the LLM is unbiased.

4 Experimental Setup

4.1 Data Collection and Annotation

We introduce a new Bangla hate speech dataset, Bangla_HateSpeech (BAHS). Initially, we scraped 8,000 comments from three online platforms: X, Facebook, and YouTube. We focus on five major hate speech domains: Gender, Entertainment, Religion, Geopolitics, and Politics. Following data cleaning and human inspection, we select 1,000 samples for each domain, resulting in a final dataset of 5,000 instances (refer to Table 1). The remaining samples are discarded due to noise, irrelevance, or quality issues. After cleaning the dataset, we apply a specific annotation strategy, described in Appendix A.1 due to space constraints. Each dataset sample includes five components: the original Bangla comment, a key area (Gender, Entertainment, Religion, Geopolitics, or Politics), a predefined label set, a human-annotated true label, and a human-written justification for that label. For example, the comment “পাপন কে জুতা দিয়ে পিটিয়ে বিসিবি থেকে বের করে দেয়া হউক” (Let Papon be beaten with shoes and thrown out of the BCB) belongs to the Gender key area, is labeled as Violence, and is justified by explicit incitement to physical harm and threats to social order. For our experiment, We design 21 identity categories distributed across five socially significant domains: Gender (e.g., Female, Male), Religion (e.g., Muslim, Hindu, Not Muslim and Hindu), Entertainment (e.g. Artist, Sportsman, Vlogger), Geopolitics and Politics (e.g., Politician, Diplomacy, Security Analyst).

4.2 Large Language Model Selection

For our experiment, we select 17 state-of-the-art LLMs from six different generative AI families: ChatGPT (OpenAI), Gemini (Google), Mistral, LLaMA (Meta), Qwen (Alibaba), and DeepSeek. Our goal is to evaluate how effectively these models perform as annotators in a low-resource setting, particularly for the Bangla language, when faced with socially sensitive and bias-prone content.

4.3 Prompting-based Domain Adaptation

We use a prompt-based evaluation strategy to simulate domain adaptation for both proprietary and open-access LLMs. We design task-specific prompts in Bangla to support domain adaptation for classification, reasoning, and taxonomy-based prompt sensitivity evaluation. For each model family, we begin with the smallest variant pretrained on general-domain data and assess its performance on identity-sensitive Bangla hate speech. If the model performs below expectation, indicated by identity mismatches, low F1 scores, or unstable reasoning, we progressively scale to larger variants within the same family. This stepwise strategy allows us to identify the smallest model capable of adapting to culturally grounded Bangla texts and to evaluate whether model scaling alone improves domain-specific performance. By combining structured prompting with progressive scaling, we establish a consistent evaluation pipeline for low-resource, culturally rich language domains.

4.4 Evaluation Framework and Metrics

To understand how LLMs behave as annotators in a low-resource language like Bangla, we design a three-dimension evaluation framework focused on bias and model behavior. This framework assesses: (i) classification of collected comments considering the identity of individuals, (ii) the reasoning ability to justify the predicted label, and (iii) the sensitivity to different levels of prompts (the prompt level is decided from different levels of directives, for example, only goal directives, goal directives with detail instructions, and, in another level, the prompt contains examples with instructions). This setup helps to reveal not just performance gaps but also deeper issues like bias amplification, inconsistency across prompts, and unreliable reasoning, which offer a well-rounded view of model reliability in sensitive annotation tasks.

4.4.1 Classification of Comments (E1)

The first dimension of our framework assesses how well each model could classify hate speech in Bangla when linked to a specific identity group. Models receive a standardized prompt framing them as expert annotators with identity cues (e.g., Female, Muslim, Artist) and are asked to choose one label from a fixed label set: Harassment, Offensive, Violence, Harmful, Propaganda, or Not Hateful. We evaluate model predictions using F1 Score for label balance, Cohen’s Kappa for agreement with human annotations, and a Mismatch metric to measure differences in responses across opposing identity terms (e.g., Female vs Not Female), highlighting potential bias in classification.

4.4.2 Reasoning Alignment (E2)

In the second dimension, we evaluate whether LLMs can generate appropriate reasoning to justify their predicted labels. Each LLM is provided with a comment in Bangla, its own predicted label (for that given comment), and a specified identity, and is asked to produce three short reasoning statements, each limited to a maximum of 10 tokens. These generated justifications are then compared against human-written rationales using two semantic similarity metrics: cosine similarity to measure contextual alignment and BERTScore to capture context-based token overlap. To ensure an accurate and fair evaluation in Bangla, we use the ‘xlm-roberta-base’ model Conneau et al. (2019), pretrained on Bangla, to compute the BERTScore. Similarly, we select the ‘paraphrase-multilingual-MiniLM-L12-v2’ model Reimers and Gurevych (2019), which is also trained on Bangla, to calculate Cosine Similarity. Both models are built for multilingual tasks and help us measure how closely the LLMs reasoning matches human judgment, highlighting whether explanations reflect true understanding or superficial patterns. This dimension is essential for evaluating how well models can justify their decisions across different identities.

4.4.3 Prompt Sensitivity (E3)

The third dimension evaluates how sensitive the models are to different levels of prompts, focusing on consistency in behavior when the model is asked to do the same task with different instructions. Using the TELeR taxonomy Santu and Feng (2023), we create four different levels of prompts: a simple directive (Level 1), a multi-sentence prompt with a goal mentioned (Level 2), bullet point instructions (Level 3), and a few-shot example with instructions (Level 4). These prompt variations are applied to evaluate the classification task (E1). We conduct this experiment in the Gender key area due to its relevance and sensitivity, as gender biases in NLP can significantly influence model outputs Blodgett et al. (2020). We evaluate 17 LLMs across the four levels of prompts, with performance measured using F1 Score and Cohen’s Kappa. This setup allow us to assess how changes in prompt structure affect model predictions, highlighting potential instability in tasks.

5 Methodology

For a structured assessment, we introduce a scoring system based on outcomes from three evaluation dimensions: E1 (Classification), E2 (Reasoning), and E3 (Prompt Sensitivity), as shown in Figure 2. Each model receives a score from 1 (weak performance) to 3 (strong performance) per dimension, enabling systematic comparison across evaluation aspects. Our goal is to analyze LLM annotation behavior and group models into human-like, adaptive, and objective annotator types. Defining meaningful performance thresholds for these categories is non-trivial and cannot be set arbitrarily. We ground threshold selection using a human annotation study (Appendix A.8) where 55 annotators label and reason over 100 representative samples under the same task definitions, allowing us to estimate expected human agreement in identity-sensitive settings. The distribution of human judgments is then used to calibrate the score boundaries for E1–E3, ensuring that the proposed scoring scheme reflects human perceptions of correctness, uncertainty, and variability rather than designer-defined thresholds.

  • •

    E1 (Classification of Comments):

    • ∘\circ

      Score 3: A model receives a score of 3 if it achieves F1 and Cohen’s Kappa scores ≥85%\geq 85\% and mismatch score for varying identity ≤5%\leq 5\%.

    • ∘\circ

      Score 2: A score of 2 for partial success (e.g., only two metrics passing thresholds).

    • ∘\circ

      Score 1: Otherwise, it receives a score of 1.

  • •

    E2 (Reasoning Alignment):

    • ∘\circ

      Score 3: A score of 3 is assigned for BERTScore and Cosine Similarity ≥95%\geq 95\%.

    • ∘\circ

      Score 2: A score of 2 for moderately high scores (between 80% and 95%).

    • ∘\circ

      Score 1: Otherwise, it receives a score of 1.

  • •

    E3 (Prompt Sensitivity): Based on the TELeR-style prompts Santu and Feng (2023), models are scored as follows:

    • ∘\circ

      Score 3: F1 and Kappa >> 50%, 60%, 70%, and 80% for prompts 1–4, respectively, and mismatch << 20%, 15%, 10%, and 5%.

    • ∘\circ

      Score 2: F1 and Kappa between 40–50%, 50–60%, 60–70%, 70–80% respectively with mismatch thresholds relaxed to 30%, 20%, 15%, and 10%.

    • ∘\circ

      Score 1: For all other cases, indicating high instability.

Based on the structured evaluation, we categorize models into three behavioral types:

  • •

    Human-like Annotators: Models that correlate with human judgments in classification and reasoning, meeting the highest thresholds across E1, E2, and E3.

  • •

    Objective Annotators: Models that perform well in at least two dimensions but may show prompt instability or weaker reasoning alignment.

  • •

    Adaptive Annotators: Models that fail to meet most thresholds, showing inconsistent behavior and high sensitivity to prompt changes.

Algorithm 1 describes how models are categorized into Human-like annotators, Objective annotators, or Adaptive annotators based on E1–E3 scores and threshold criteria.

6 Results

We conduct a comprehensive evaluation of 17 state-of-the-art LLMs on Bangla texts spanning 21 identity-sensitive categories (e.g., Female, Not Female, Hindu, Artist etc.) across five domains (e.g., Gender, Religion, Entertainment etc.). The result shows that modern LLMs struggle with the classification of hateful comments task (E1) despite their large scale. Large-scale models such as GPT-4o Mini and Gemini 2.0 Flash Lite often underperform, achieving F1 scores below 45% (refer to Figure 3(a), row 10 and column 11) and Cohen’s Kappa values near 50% (refer to Figure 5, row 10 and column 11 in appendix), particularly on sensitive categories such as Politician, Security Analyst, and Diplomat. For example, GPT-4o Mini obtains an F1-score of 42.4% (refer to Figure 3(a), row 10 and column 9) and Cohen’s Kappa 42.1% (refer to Figure 5, row 10 and column 9 in appendix) with an identity of Politician.

In contrast, smaller models such as Qwen 2.5 (7B) show more consistent result, with F1 score above 41% (refer to Figure 3(a), row 1 and column 2) and identity-based mismatch rates as low as 0.86% in binary contrasts, for example, Female vs Not Female. DeepSeek R1 Distill (70B) also performs reliably, maintaining F1 score above 44% (refer to Figure 3(a), row 1 and column 17) and mismatch below 2.15% (refer to Table 8 in the Appendix). Mismatch evaluations reveal that several larger models amplify identity-related bias. GPT-3.5 Turbo exhibits extreme variation, as exemplified by a 31.45% mismatch in the “Journalist vs. Not Journalist” classification, highlighting a trend we term Bias Amplification through identity framing (refer to Table 8 in the Appendix). Interestingly, we find that most LLMs struggle with the Politician vs. Not Politician category in the Politics domain. Political identity is highly dynamic and most LLMs cannot adapt to evolving political roles due to being trained on static web data.

In the reasoning alignment task (E2), most models achieve high similarity scores, with BERTScore above 94% (refer to Figure 3(b), row 1 and column 2) and cosine similarity above 97% (refer to Figure 8, row 1 and column 2 in appendix), even when their classification performance (E1) is weak. This gap indicates that LLMs can generate fluent, contextually aligned explanations that resemble reference reasoning, while still failing to correctly perform hate speech classification. Only a small subset of models, such as DeepSeek R1 Distill (70B) and Gemini 1.5 Pro, consistently maintain strong performance across both reasoning and classification for all identity categories. In contrast, all other models including DeepSeek R1 Distill (8B) and Mistral (7B) perform poorly in both dimensions, with errors becoming more pronounced in identity-sensitive cases. This divergence is illustrated in Figure 3(b), highlighting that reasoning fluency alone is insufficient for reliable annotation in bias-sensitive settings.

In prompt sensitivity evaluation (E3), we evaluate models based on the TELeR taxonomy Santu and Feng (2023), assessing sensitivity to prompt variation within the Gender domain. Robust models, like DeepSeek R1 Distill (70B) and O1, maintain high F1 and Kappa (above 75% and 85%) with a mismatch under 3% across all prompt levels, i.e., Level 1 through Level 4, which are closer to the Human-like Annotator standard. In contrast, models such as Mixtral Instruct (56B), Gemini 2.0 Flash Lite, and GPT-3.5 Turbo show high prompt sensitivity and mismatch rates exceeding 26% and poor classification stability, placing them in the least reliable category (refer to Figure 11 in appendix). To further analyze prompt robustness, Figure 4 presents the distribution of model performance across prompt variants using boxplots. Models with narrower interquartile ranges (e.g., Llama 3.3, O1) demonstrate greater robustness, indicating more consistent annotation behavior under prompt variation. In contrast, models with wider dispersion (e.g., Mixtral Instruct 56B) show more sensitivity to prompt phrasing, reflecting instability during annotation. We find similar patterns in negative identities as well and include the results in the Appendix due to space constraints (Appendix 5 to 16).

Our analysis shows that smaller models such as DeepSeek R1 Distill (8B) and Qwen 2.5 (7B) often outperform larger ones such as GPT-3.5 Turbo and Gemini 2.0 Flash, especially in classification and prompt stability, selected for category 2 (Objective Annotators). Models like GPT-3.5 Turbo, Mixtral Instruct (56B), and Gemini 2.0 Flash Lite fall into Category 3 (Adaptive Annotators), underperforming on all tasks with poor accuracy, unstable reasoning, and high prompt sensitivity, making them unsuitable for fair and reliable annotation in low-resource languages like Bangla, as shown in Table 3. In summary, LLMs still struggle to accurately annotate identity-sensitive hate speech content in low-resource languages due to their biased training data and poor generalization in these languages [answers RQ 1]. Although LLMs show strong reasoning abilities, our experiments reveal that their reasoning is not always reliable. They perform poorly on classification and are highly sensitive to identity as well as prompts, meaning an LLM can still provide convincing justifications even for an incorrect label [answers RQ 2].

7 Discussion and Conclusion

This work provides a systematic analysis of LLMs as annotators for identity-sensitive hate speech task in a low-resource language and yields several important insights. First, model scale does not reliably indicate annotation quality. In many cases, smaller and more task-aligned models (e.g., Qwen 2.5 7B) outperform larger models (e.g., GPT-3.5 Turbo) in both accuracy and consistency, indicating that scale alone is a poor indicator of reliability. Second, we observe a disconnect between explanation fluency and labeling correctness: several models generate confident and well-structured reasoning while assigning incorrect labels, showing that reasoning quality is not a reliable proxy for correct annotation. Third, model behavior is highly sensitive to prompt formulation, where minor wording leads to inconsistent outputs. Fourth, performance varies sharply across identity pairs, with most models failing to achieve even average accuracy for contrasts such as politician vs. non-politician, indicating systematic weaknesses in fine-grained identity discrimination.

These challenges are further amplified by the linguistic and contextual characteristics of Bangla, which increase semantic ambiguity in identity-sensitive cases. Under our three-stage evaluation framework, no model achieves human-level reliability across classification, reasoning, and robustness. While a few larger models reach average overall performance, they often exhibit stronger identity-specific bias than smaller counterparts, as observed for DeepSeek R1 Distill 70B relative to Qwen 2.5 7B. Overall, most LLMs fall into the adaptive annotator category due to unstable behavior, suggesting that current systems remain promising but insufficient as standalone annotators for sensitive tasks in low-resource languages.

Limitations

While our evaluation framework provides a comprehensive insight into the behavior of LLMs in Bangla hate speech annotation, several limitations remain. First, our analysis is constrained to Bangla, a single low-resource language. Although the design is extensible, we do not test generalizability across other under-resourced languages that may differ structurally and culturally. Second, our prompt-based evaluation relies on manually crafted templates, which, while controlled, may not reflect the full range of user phrasing seen in real-world annotation settings. This may limit ecological validity. Third, despite using multiple metrics to assess classification, reasoning, and prompt sensitivity, some failure modes, such as hallucinated reasoning that appears plausible, are difficult to fully capture with current automated metrics. Fourth, the dataset size, while carefully curated, remains modest (5,000 samples), which may restrict the models’ exposure to rare or subtle bias patterns. Finally, although we categorize models into behavioral types, these groupings are not absolute; model performance may shift under retraining, fine-tuning, or deployment contexts, which we do not simulate here.

Future work should address these limitations by expanding language coverage, incorporating more dynamic prompting methods, refining evaluation metrics for reasoning alignment task (as BERTscore and cosine-similarity tend to saturate and highly rely on transformer-based models), and validating model behavior in practical annotation workflows.

Appendix A Appendix

A.1 Dataset Annotation

To annotate the data samples in our proposed dataset, we define six output labels - ‘Offensive’, ‘Sexual Harassment’, ‘Violence’, ‘Harmful’, ‘Propaganda’, and ‘Not Hateful’, where five labels represent different forms of hate speech and the sixth represents neutral or non-hateful comments. To ensure fairness and minimize bias in the annotation process, we employ a majority voting method. Three graduate students, who are domain experts, are selected as annotators. They vote to assign one of the six labels to each comment (actual text). Each annotator also provides three individual short justifications (reasoning) in Bangla for the chosen label, explaining why it is the most appropriate label for the comment.

After annotation, each sample in the dataset contains five attributes - the actual text (collected comments), key areas (Gender, Entertainment, Religion, Geopolitics, and Politics), a set of labels (six labels as options for classifying different types of hateful comments), the correct label (human-annotated true label), and the reasoning for that label (human-annotated justification). For example, a data sample with the actual text, “পাপন কে জুতা দিয়ে পিটিয়ে বিসিবি থেকে বের করে দেয়া হউক” (Let Papon be beaten with shoes and thrown out of the BCB), is from the key area ‘Gender’, has the true label ‘Violence’, and the reasons for labeling the text as ‘Violence’ are: “মন্তব্যটি সরাসরি সহিংসতার আহ্বান জানিয়েছে, যা সম্পূর্ণ অপ্রত্যাশিত। শারীরিক আঘাত এবং অপমানসূচক মনোভাবের কারণে এটি অগ্রহণযোগ্য। এটি হিংসাত্মক এবং সামাজিক শৃঙ্খলার জন্য হুমকি।” (The comment explicitly incites violence, making it highly offensive and unacceptable. It promotes physical harm, carries a disrespectful tone, and poses a serious threat to social order).

Although the annotation label set contains contains five labels for hateful content and only one for neutral content, we maintain a balanced distribution in the dataset. Specifically, 50% of the samples represent hateful content, while the remaining 50% consist of neutral text, ensuring that the dataset remains unbiased. The reason for selecting multiple labels for hateful content is to evaluate whether LLMs may get confused and hallucinate, similar to humans. There is often contextual and surface-level overlap between these labels, with differences usually coming down to small details such as tone, intent, or context that may not be immediately obvious.

A.2 Label Design and Taxonomy

To capture the subtle variations of harmful speech in Bangla, we constructed a six-class label taxonomy: Sexual Harassment, Offensive, Violence, Harmful, Propaganda, and Not Hateful. These labels were deliberately chosen to reflect fine-grained, overlapping semantic meanings that would challenge the discriminatory ability of language models. Our goal was to test whether models could distinguish harmful intent from contextual subtleties and whether close label proximity would lead to confusion in prediction.

A.3 Identity Categories and Grouping

We designed 21 identity categories distributed across five socially significant domains: Gender (e.g., Female, Male), Religion (e.g., Muslim, Hindu, Not Muslim, and Hindu), Entertainment (e.g. Artist, Sportsman, Vlogger), Politics and Power (e.g., Politician, Diplomacy, Security Analyst). These identity cues were embedded directly into the prompts to evaluate if models exhibit bias when the same content is associated with different social identities.

A.4 Evaluation Metrics

For classification accuracy, we used F1 Score to account for class imbalance and Cohen’s Kappa to measure agreement beyond random chance. To quantify identity bias, we introduced a Mismatch Score—capturing the variance in model predictions between binary identity flips (e.g., Female vs Not Female). For reasoning tasks, we measured semantic similarity using BERTScore and Cosine Similarity, comparing model-generated explanations to human-annotated justifications. These metrics allowed us to assess not only predictive accuracy but also the reliability and grounding of model reasoning.

A.5 Prompt Variation and Stability Testing

We evaluated prompt sensitivity using four variations inspired by the TELeR taxonomy: (1) a simple one-line directive, (2) a multi-sentence goal, (3) a bullet-point instruction list, and (4) a few-shot example-based prompt. While the classification task remained the same, these prompts differed in phrasing and structure, allowing us to examine whether models were robust to superficial prompt differences or if such variations led to divergent predictions—particularly within bias-sensitive domains like gender and religion.

A.6 Label Ablation Analysis

To test label confusion, we conducted a label ablation study using the smallest model from each LLM family. Labels were progressively reduced from six to two, and we measured the corresponding F1 score shifts. Across all LLMs, we observed improved accuracy as the label set became more distinct, with the removal of the “Offensive” class yielding the most significant performance gains. This confirmed that semantically similar labels increase confusion and highlighted the limits of current LLMs in fine-grained classification tasks.

A.7 System Environment

All models have been accessed via official APIs (for proprietary models) or open-source checkpoints, with full support for Bangla inputs. To ensure fairness and reproducibility, we standardize the generation settings, such as temperature, top p, and max tokens, and use automated scoring with manual checks on edge cases for validation. All evaluations are run on Kaggle using dual NVIDIA T4 GPUs, enabling efficient inference at scale. We test 17 LLMs across 21 identity categories, resulting in a comprehensive benchmark for cross-model and cross-category bias analysis.

A.8 Human Annotation Study

We conduct a human annotation study to estimate expected human agreement under identity-sensitive hate speech scenarios, where disagreement is common. We collect 100 representative samples spanning five key identity domains and recruit 55 annotators from culturally diverse backgrounds. Annotators are asked to independently label and reason about each sample following the same task definitions used in our experiments. Inter-annotator agreement statistics were then computed to estimate upper-bound human consistency under realistic disagreement conditions.

A.9 Supplementary Figures and Visualizations

The appendix includes key figures cited in the paper, i.e., performance heatmaps (F1, Kappa), reasoning similarity charts, mismatch scores across identity pairs, prompt-level bias visualizations, and the label ablation graph. Each figure is presented with clear captions and reflects the results across 17 LLMs, showing model performance trends, vulnerabilities, and behavioral shifts across the three evaluation dimensions.
